ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the Ethics and Research Committee in Obafemi Awolowo University Teaching Hospitals Complex (Protocol Number: ERC/2024/06/22) and the School of Medicine Research Ethics Committee, Cardiff University (SREC Reference: 24/30).
We recruited 320 twin pairs (aged 3-5 years) and both parents in two Nigerian towns.

Participants were assessed for MHSs (emotional/behavioural symptoms in children; anxiety, depressive and Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder symptoms in parents), and selected risk/protective factors (adverse home environments, adverse childhood experiences, poor physical health; and religiosity, parental warmth and prosociality).

To bridge these gaps, we recruited a genetically informative sample of parents and preschool twin children in Nigeria and investigated: i. associations between paternal and maternal MHSs (depressive, anxiety and Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder [ADHD] symptoms) and child MHSs (behavioural; and emotional symptoms); ii. mediation of parentchild MHS associations by measured risk (household chaos, intimate partner violence, adverse childhood experiences and children's poor physical health)/protective (parental warmth, parents' religiosity and children's prosocial behaviour) factors, and iii. overall genetic and environmental influences on childhood MHSs, and how parental MHSs impact these.
Parents provided informed consent for themselves and their children.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Ninety percent of the world's children live in Low-/Middle-Income Countries (LMICs), but relatively little is known about children's mental health risk in these settings.

Using a genetically informative twin-family design, we estimated parent-child associations for mental health symptoms (MHSs), indirect effects through specific risk/protective factors, and how parental MHSs impact genetic/environmental influences on child MHSs in Nigeria.
We recruited 320 twin pairs (aged 3-5 years) and both parents in two Nigerian towns.

Participants were assessed for MHSs (emotional/behavioural symptoms in children; anxiety, depressive and Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder symptoms in parents), and selected risk/protective factors (adverse home environments, adverse childhood experiences, poor physical health; and religiosity, parental warmth and prosociality).
We used structural equation modelling to test parent-child MHS associations, and mediation by risk/protective factors.
We estimated latent genetic (A), shared environmental (C) and individual-specific environmental (E) influences on child MHSs, and how parent MHSs impact these influences using univariate twin models.
Child MHSs were significantly associated with MHSs in both parents.
The strongest indirect effects for parent-child MHS associations were through adverse childhood experiences and diminished parental warmth.
Others indirect pathways involved poor physical health and diminished prosociality.
Latent A and C influences each explained 22-29% of the individual differences in children's MHSs.
Independent of A influences, C influences were impacted by parents' MHSs.

Our findings indicate that potentially modifiable environmental pathways are important for understanding parent-child MHS associations for very young children in a LMIC, and these may inform intervention design.
Larger and more rigorous genetically informative designs are needed to replicate and extend our findings.
Up to one in every six children in the world experiences significant mental health (including neurodevelopmental) symptoms (MHSs) (Kieling et al., 2024).

In contrast, there were only minimal changes in the additive genetic and individual-specific environmental components.
To our knowledge, this is the first study to investigate pathways between parental and childhood MHSs in sub-Saharan Africa using a genetically sensitive family-based design.

Paternal and maternal MHSs were significantly associated with childhood MHSs (behavioural and emotional symptoms), as were specific risk factors (adverse home environments indexed by intimate partner violence and household chaos, adverse childhood experiences [ACEs] and children's poor physical health) and diminished protective factors (parental warmth and prosociality).
In the final models incorporating both parents' MHSs and all the risk/protective factors for each childhood MHS, ACEs and low prosociality mediated the associations with both childhood MHSs.
In addition, children's poor physical health and low parental warmth further mediated the associations with emotional symptoms.

Finally, biometric analyses indicated moderate additive genetic and shared environmental influences on childhood MHSs, and parental MHSs impacted on shared environmental influences on childhood MHSs independent of genetic influences.
Consistent with existing research, childhood MHSs were significantly associated with paternal and maternal MHSs (Jami et al., 2021; Scarlett et al., 2024).

text.text: Using genetically informative data, we provide preliminary estimates of genetic and environmental influences on early childhood MHSs in a LMIC setting; and explored how these influences impact on parent-child MHS associations.
Despite these strengths, our findings need to be interpreted considering the following limitations.

Although our absolute sample size was large (1230 adults and children), adjusting for clustering reduced this to 320 household units (and twin pairs), which may be underpowered to detect small effects (including estimates of A and C influences on child MHSs) as evidenced by wide confidence intervals.

What's known?
 Parental mental health symptoms (MHSs) are strong risk factors for childhood MHSs.
What's new?

 Using a genetically informative design in a Nigerian sample, we identified key risk (adverse childhood experiences and children's poor physical health) and diminished protective (prosociality and parental warmth) factors that partly explained parent-child MHS associations.
 The shared environment is an important component of parent-child MHS associations in our LMIC sample, independent of genetic influences.
 We highlighted key risk and protective factors relevant for understanding childhood MHSs in a LMIC.
 Future childhood MHS research in LMICs should use larger genetically informative samples to allow causal inference.
